Problem Statement, Objectives and Experimental Configuration¶

Problem Statement¶

A consortium of hospitals wishes to train a shared image-classification model without exchanging private local data. This notebook simulates that setting using five federated clients. Each client trains locally and shares only model parameters, which are aggregated centrally using a manually implemented Federated Averaging algorithm.

MNIST is used as the required image-classification dataset. The hospital scenario represents the privacy-preserving motivation; no real patient data are used.

Objectives¶

  1. Prepare MNIST and create five IID and five Non-IID client partitions.
  2. Develop a compact CNN and train it locally at each simulated client.
  3. Implement sample-weighted FedAvg manually without a federated-learning framework.
  4. Run ten communication rounds and record client and global metrics.
  5. Compare local epochs 1, 2, and 5.
  6. Compare IID and Non-IID convergence, global accuracy, loss, and class-wise performance.
  7. Critically analyze client heterogeneity and propose an improvement over standard FedAvg.

Experimental Configuration¶

Component Setting
Clients 5
Communication rounds 10
Batch size 32
Main local epochs 2
Epoch comparison 1, 2, 5
Model Lightweight CNN
Optimizer Adam
Loss Sparse categorical cross-entropy
Aggregation Manual sample-count-weighted FedAvg
Evaluation Central MNIST test set

3. MNIST Dataset Loading¶

The MNIST handwritten-digit dataset is loaded using the TensorFlow/Keras dataset utility. It contains 60,000 training images and 10,000 testing images across 10 digit classes. The training data will later be divided among five simulated federated clients, while the test data will be retained for evaluating the global model.

In [3]:

4. Initial Visual Inspection of MNIST Samples¶

A selection of handwritten-digit images is displayed to verify the visual content, image orientation, background convention, and correspondence between images and labels. This qualitative inspection provides an initial understanding of the dataset before performing quantitative exploratory data analysis.

The displayed samples should not be interpreted as representative of the complete class distribution because they are taken from only a small subset of the training data. Class balance, pixel characteristics, data quality, and inter-class variation are analysed separately in subsequent sections.

5. Class Distribution Analysis¶

The frequency of each digit class is examined separately for the training and testing datasets. This analysis determines whether the dataset is balanced and whether any class is underrepresented.

Class imbalance can influence classification performance because classes with more samples may contribute more frequently to gradient updates. In federated learning, the original class distribution is also important because it forms the basis for creating IID and Non-IID client partitions.

In [5]:
# Calculate class frequencies for the training and testing datasets
train_class_counts = np.bincount(y_train, minlength=10)
test_class_counts = np.bincount(y_test, minlength=10)

class_distribution = pd.DataFrame({
    "Digit": np.arange(10),
    "Training Samples": train_class_counts,
    "Training Percentage": (train_class_counts / len(y_train)) * 100,
    "Testing Samples": test_class_counts,
    "Testing Percentage": (test_class_counts / len(y_test)) * 100
})

class_distribution["Train-Test Percentage Difference"] = (
    class_distribution["Training Percentage"]
    - class_distribution["Testing Percentage"]
).abs()

print("=" * 100)
print("MNIST CLASS DISTRIBUTION")
print("=" * 100)

display(
    class_distribution.style.format({
        "Training Percentage": "{:.2f}%",
        "Testing Percentage": "{:.2f}%",
        "Train-Test Percentage Difference": "{:.2f}%"
    })
)

print("\nSUMMARY STATISTICS")
print("-" * 100)

print(f"Most frequent training class : {train_class_counts.argmax()} "
      f"({train_class_counts.max()} samples)")

print(f"Least frequent training class: {train_class_counts.argmin()} "
      f"({train_class_counts.min()} samples)")

print(f"Training imbalance ratio     : "
      f"{train_class_counts.max() / train_class_counts.min():.4f}")

print(f"Most frequent testing class  : {test_class_counts.argmax()} "
      f"({test_class_counts.max()} samples)")

print(f"Least frequent testing class : {test_class_counts.argmin()} "
      f"({test_class_counts.min()} samples)")

print(f"Testing imbalance ratio      : "
      f"{test_class_counts.max() / test_class_counts.min():.4f}")

# Visualise training and testing class counts
x_positions = np.arange(10)
bar_width = 0.38

plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6))

plt.bar(
    x_positions - bar_width / 2,
    train_class_counts,
    width=bar_width,
    label="Training Set"
)

plt.bar(
    x_positions + bar_width / 2,
    test_class_counts,
    width=bar_width,
    label="Testing Set"
)

plt.title("Class Distribution in MNIST Training and Testing Datasets", fontsize=14)
plt.xlabel("Digit Class")
plt.ylabel("Number of Samples")

plt.legend()

6. Data Quality and Integrity Validation¶

This section performs structural and data-quality checks on the MNIST training and testing datasets. The objective is to verify that the arrays contain valid image dimensions, expected labels, finite values, valid pixel intensities, and no completely blank images.

These checks are important because invalid samples, unexpected labels, or corrupted pixel values could affect local client training and produce misleading federated-learning results.

In [6]:
# Validate the structural integrity and quality of the MNIST dataset

expected_image_shape = (28, 28)
expected_classes = np.arange(10)

train_unique_labels = np.unique(y_train)
test_unique_labels = np.unique(y_test)

train_nan_count = np.isnan(x_train).sum()
test_nan_count = np.isnan(x_test).sum()

train_inf_count = np.isinf(x_train).sum()
test_inf_count = np.isinf(x_test).sum()

train_blank_images = np.sum(np.count_nonzero(x_train, axis=(1, 2)) == 0)
test_blank_images = np.sum(np.count_nonzero(x_test, axis=(1, 2)) == 0)

train_invalid_pixel_count = np.sum((x_train < 0) | (x_train > 255))
test_invalid_pixel_count = np.sum((x_test < 0) | (x_test > 255))

quality_checks = pd.DataFrame({
    "Validation Check": [
        "Training image shape",
        "Testing image shape",
        "Training labels",
        "Testing labels",
        "Training NaN values",
        "Testing NaN values",
        "Training infinite values",
        "Testing infinite values",
        "Training blank images",
        "Testing blank images",
        "Training invalid pixels",
        "Testing invalid pixels"
    ],
    "Observed Value": [
        str(x_train.shape[1:]),
        str(x_test.shape[1:]),
        str(train_unique_labels.tolist()),
        str(test_unique_labels.tolist()),
        int(train_nan_count),
        int(test_nan_count),
        int(train_inf_count),
        int(test_inf_count),
        int(train_blank_images),
        int(test_blank_images),
        int(train_invalid_pixel_count),
        int(test_invalid_pixel_count)
    ],
    "Expected Condition": [
        str(expected_image_shape),
        str(expected_image_shape),
        str(expected_classes.tolist()),
        str(expected_classes.tolist()),
        "0",
        "0",
        "0",
        "0",
        "0",
        "0",
        "0",
        "0"
    ]
})

quality_checks["Status"] = [
    "Pass" if x_train.shape[1:] == expected_image_shape else "Fail",
    "Pass" if x_test.shape[1:] == expected_image_shape else "Fail",
    "Pass" if np.array_equal(train_unique_labels, expected_classes) else "Fail",
    "Pass" if np.array_equal(test_unique_labels, expected_classes) else "Fail",
    "Pass" if train_nan_count == 0 else "Fail",
    "Pass" if test_nan_count == 0 else "Fail",
    "Pass" if train_inf_count == 0 else "Fail",
    "Pass" if test_inf_count == 0 else "Fail",
    "Pass" if train_blank_images == 0 else "Fail",
    "Pass" if test_blank_images == 0 else "Fail",
    "Pass" if train_invalid_pixel_count == 0 else "Fail",
    "Pass" if test_invalid_pixel_count == 0 else "Fail"
]

print("=" * 100)
print("MNIST DATA QUALITY AND INTEGRITY VALIDATION")
print("=" * 100)

display(quality_checks)

passed_checks = (quality_checks["Status"] == "Pass").sum()
total_checks = len(quality_checks)

print("\nSUMMARY")
print("-" * 100)
print(f"Checks passed         : {passed_checks}/{total_checks}")
print(f"Training samples      : {len(x_train)}")
print(f"Testing samples       : {len(x_test)}")
print(f"Image dimensions      : {x_train.shape[1]} x {x_train.shape[2]}")
print(f"Valid label range     : {train_unique_labels.min()} to {train_unique_labels.max()}")
print(f"Pixel intensity range : {x_train.min()} to {x_train.max()}")

if passed_checks == total_checks:
    print("\nValidation status     : All dataset integrity checks passed.")
else:
    print("\nValidation status     : One or more integrity checks failed.")

7. Pixel Intensity Distribution Analysis¶

The distribution of grayscale pixel intensities is analysed to understand the relationship between image background and handwritten foreground strokes.

MNIST images contain a large black background area and a smaller number of non-zero pixels representing the handwritten digit. Examining the pixel distribution helps determine the extent of sparsity, the prevalence of background pixels, and whether normalization is required before model training.

The analysis is performed separately for the training and testing datasets to verify that both datasets exhibit similar low-level image characteristics.

In [7]:
# Analyse pixel intensity distributions in the training and testing datasets

train_pixels = x_train.reshape(-1)
test_pixels = x_test.reshape(-1)

train_zero_pixels = np.sum(train_pixels == 0)
test_zero_pixels = np.sum(test_pixels == 0)

train_nonzero_pixels = np.sum(train_pixels > 0)
test_nonzero_pixels = np.sum(test_pixels > 0)

train_total_pixels = train_pixels.size
test_total_pixels = test_pixels.size

pixel_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": [
        "Total pixels",
        "Zero-valued pixels",
        "Non-zero pixels",
        "Zero-pixel percentage",
        "Non-zero pixel percentage",
        "Mean pixel intensity",
        "Median pixel intensity",
        "Standard deviation",
        "Minimum intensity",
        "Maximum intensity"
    ],
    "Training Set": [
        train_total_pixels,
        train_zero_pixels,
        train_nonzero_pixels,
        (train_zero_pixels / train_total_pixels) * 100,
        (train_nonzero_pixels / train_total_pixels) * 100,
        train_pixels.mean(),
        np.median(train_pixels),
        train_pixels.std(),
        train_pixels.min(),
        train_pixels.max()
    ],
    "Testing Set": [
        test_total_pixels,
        test_zero_pixels,
        test_nonzero_pixels,
        (test_zero_pixels / test_total_pixels) * 100,
        (test_nonzero_pixels / test_total_pixels) * 100,
        test_pixels.mean(),
        np.median(test_pixels),
        test_pixels.std(),
        test_pixels.min(),
        test_pixels.max()
    ]
})

print("=" * 100)
print("PIXEL INTENSITY DISTRIBUTION SUMMARY")
print("=" * 100)

display(
    pixel_summary.style.format({
        "Training Set": "{:,.4f}",
        "Testing Set": "{:,.4f}"
    })
)

# Plot pixel intensity histograms
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6))

plt.hist(
    train_pixels,
    bins=50,
    density=True,
    alpha=0.6,
    label="Training Set"
)

plt.hist(
    test_pixels,
    bins=50,
    density=True,
    alpha=0.6,
    label="Testing Set"
)

plt.title("Pixel Intensity Distribution in MNIST")
plt.xlabel("Pixel Intensity")
plt.ylabel("Density")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.4)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("\nADDITIONAL SUMMARY")
print("-" * 100)

print(
    f"Training background proportion : "
    f"{(train_zero_pixels / train_total_pixels) * 100:.2f}%"
)

print(
    f"Testing background proportion  : "
    f"{(test_zero_pixels / test_total_pixels) * 100:.2f}%"
)

print(
    f"Training foreground proportion : "
    f"{(train_nonzero_pixels / train_total_pixels) * 100:.2f}%"
)

print(
    f"Testing foreground proportion  : "
    f"{(test_nonzero_pixels / test_total_pixels) * 100:.2f}%"
)

Observations¶

  • Approximately 80.88% of training pixels and 80.72% of testing pixels are zero-valued background; the remaining 19.12% and 19.28% represent foreground stroke information.
  • Training and testing intensity profiles are closely aligned, so no low-level pixel-distribution shift is evident.
  • A fixed 0–255 to 0–1 rescaling is used because the source range is known, it preserves the zero background, and it retains the relative grayscale contrast needed by the CNN.

8. Image-Level Brightness and Foreground Analysis¶

This section examines image-level characteristics rather than aggregating all pixels together. For every image, the mean pixel intensity and number of non-zero foreground pixels are calculated.

The purpose is to understand how much handwriting area and brightness vary across samples and digit classes. These characteristics provide insight into intra-class variability and help identify whether certain classes consistently occupy more or less image area.

In [8]:
# Calculate image-level brightness and foreground statistics

train_mean_intensity = x_train.mean(axis=(1, 2))
test_mean_intensity = x_test.mean(axis=(1, 2))

train_nonzero_count = np.count_nonzero(x_train, axis=(1, 2))
test_nonzero_count = np.count_nonzero(x_test, axis=(1, 2))

image_level_summary = pd.DataFrame({

        "Mean image intensity",

    ],
    "Training Set": [
        train_mean_intensity.mean(),

        np.median(train_nonzero_count),
        train_nonzero_count.min(),
        train_nonzero_count.max()
    ],

        test_mean_intensity.mean(),

        test_nonzero_count.mean(),
        np.median(test_nonzero_count),
        test_nonzero_count.min(),
        test_nonzero_count.max()
    ]
})

9. Class-Average Image Analysis¶

Average images are computed for each digit class by taking the pixel-wise mean of all training images belonging to that class.

These average representations reveal the dominant spatial structure learned from thousands of handwritten samples. They help identify the common stroke patterns, central alignment, class-level variability, and areas where different classes may visually overlap.

In [9]:
# Compute and display the average image for each digit class

class_average_images = []

for digit in range(10):
    class_images = x_train[y_train == digit]
    average_image = class_images.mean(axis=0)
    class_average_images.append(average_image)

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 6))

for digit, average_image in enumerate(class_average_images):
    plt.subplot(2, 5, digit + 1)
    plt.imshow(average_image, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)
    plt.title(f"Average Digit: {digit}")
    plt.axis("off")

plt.suptitle(
    "Pixel-Wise Average Image for Each MNIST Digit Class",
    fontsize=15,
    y=1.02
)
plt.tight_layout()

for digit, average_image in enumerate(class_average_images):

        "Average Image Maximum Intensity": average_image.max(),

10. Data Preprocessing and Normalization¶

The MNIST images are converted from unsigned 8-bit integers to 32-bit floating-point values and normalized from the original range of 0–255 to 0–1.

A channel dimension is also added so that every image has the shape 28 × 28 × 1, which is required by the convolutional neural network. The same preprocessing is applied to both the training and testing datasets to maintain consistency during local client training and global model evaluation.

In [10]:
# Preserve the original arrays and create preprocessed copies
x_train_processed = x_train.astype("float32") / 255.0
x_test_processed = x_test.astype("float32") / 255.0

# Add the grayscale channel dimension required by Conv2D
x_train_processed = np.expand_dims(x_train_processed, axis=-1)
x_test_processed = np.expand_dims(x_test_processed, axis=-1)

print("=" * 100)

print("=" * 100)

print(f"Processed training shape    : {x_train_processed.shape}")
print(f"Original testing shape      : {x_test.shape}")
print(f"Processed testing shape     : {x_test_processed.shape}")

print(f"\nOriginal training dtype     : {x_train.dtype}")
print(f"Processed training dtype    : {x_train_processed.dtype}")
print(f"Original testing dtype      : {x_test.dtype}")
print(f"Processed testing dtype     : {x_test_processed.dtype}")

print(
    f"\nProcessed training range    : "
    f"{x_train_processed.min():.4f} to {x_train_processed.max():.4f}"
)

print(
    f"Processed testing range     : "
    f"{x_test_processed.min():.4f} to {x_test_processed.max():.4f}"
)

print(f"Training labels shape       : {y_train.shape}")
print(f"Testing labels shape        : {y_test.shape}")

shape_valid = (
    x_train_processed.shape == (60000, 28, 28, 1)
    and x_test_processed.shape == (10000, 28, 28, 1)
)

range_valid = (
    x_train_processed.min() >= 0.0
    and x_train_processed.max() <= 1.0
    and x_test_processed.min() >= 0.0
    and x_test_processed.max() <= 1.0
)

dtype_valid = (
    x_train_processed.dtype == np.float32
    and x_test_processed.dtype == np.float32
)

print(f"Pixel range validation     : {'Pass' if range_valid else 'Fail'}")

if shape_valid and range_valid and dtype_valid:

11. IID Client Data Partitioning¶

The preprocessed MNIST training dataset is divided among five simulated federated clients using an Independent and Identically Distributed (IID) strategy.

The training indices are shuffled using a fixed random seed and then split equally across the clients. This allows each client to receive a representative mixture of all ten digit classes while preserving reproducibility.

In [11]:
# Create five IID client partitions

NUM_CLIENTS = 5

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

all_indices = np.arange(len(x_train_processed))
shuffled_indices = rng.permutation(all_indices)

iid_index_splits = np.array_split(shuffled_indices, NUM_CLIENTS)

iid_clients = {}

for client_id, client_indices in enumerate(iid_index_splits, start=1):
    iid_clients[f"Client_{client_id}"] = {
        "x": x_train_processed[client_indices],
        "y": y_train[client_indices],
        "indices": client_indices
    }

print("=" * 100)
print("IID CLIENT PARTITIONING SUMMARY")
print("=" * 100)

iid_partition_summary = []

for client_name, client_data in iid_clients.items():
    class_counts = np.bincount(client_data["y"], minlength=10)

    iid_partition_summary.append({
        "Client": client_name,
        "Total Samples": len(client_data["y"]),
        **{f"Digit {digit}": class_counts[digit] for digit in range(10)}
    })

iid_partition_summary = pd.DataFrame(iid_partition_summary)

display(iid_partition_summary)

total_assigned_samples = sum(
    len(client_data["y"])
    for client_data in iid_clients.values()
)

unique_assigned_indices = np.unique(
    np.concatenate([
        client_data["indices"]
        for client_data in iid_clients.values()
    ])
)

print("\nVALIDATION RESULTS")
print("-" * 100)
print(f"Number of clients          : {len(iid_clients)}")
print(f"Samples per client         : {[len(data['y']) for data in iid_clients.values()]}")
print(f"Total assigned samples     : {total_assigned_samples}")
print(f"Unique assigned samples    : {len(unique_assigned_indices)}")
print(f"Original training samples  : {len(x_train_processed)}")

partition_valid = (
    len(iid_clients) == NUM_CLIENTS
    and total_assigned_samples == len(x_train_processed)
    and len(unique_assigned_indices) == len(x_train_processed)
)

print(
    f"\nIID partition status       : "
    f"{'Valid' if partition_valid else 'Invalid'}"
)

12. IID Client Class Distribution Visualisation¶

The class distribution of each IID client is visualised to verify that all clients contain a similar proportion of the ten digit classes.

A correctly constructed IID partition should preserve the overall MNIST class pattern across clients, with only small differences caused by random sampling.

13. Non-IID Client Data Partitioning¶

A Non-IID client distribution is created using a label-shard strategy. The training samples are first ordered by digit label and then divided into multiple shards. Each client receives two shards, resulting in client datasets dominated by a limited subset of classes.

This partition simulates realistic federated-learning environments in which different clients hold data with different label distributions.

In [13]:
# Create five Non-IID client partitions using label shards

NUM_SHARDS = 10
SHARDS_PER_CLIENT = 2

# Sort all training indices by class label
sorted_indices = np.argsort(y_train)

# Divide the label-sorted indices into equal shards
non_iid_shards = np.array_split(sorted_indices, NUM_SHARDS)

# Shuffle shard assignments reproducibly
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
shard_order = rng.permutation(NUM_SHARDS)

non_iid_clients = {}

for client_index in range(NUM_CLIENTS):
    assigned_shard_ids = shard_order[
        client_index * SHARDS_PER_CLIENT:
        (client_index + 1) * SHARDS_PER_CLIENT
    ]

    client_indices = np.concatenate([
        non_iid_shards[shard_id]
        for shard_id in assigned_shard_ids
    ])

    non_iid_clients[f"Client_{client_index + 1}"] = {
        "x": x_train_processed[client_indices],
        "y": y_train[client_indices],
        "indices": client_indices,
        "shards": assigned_shard_ids
    }

print("=" * 100)
print("NON-IID CLIENT PARTITIONING SUMMARY")
print("=" * 100)

non_iid_partition_summary = []

for client_name, client_data in non_iid_clients.items():
    class_counts = np.bincount(client_data["y"], minlength=10)

    non_iid_partition_summary.append({
        "Client": client_name,
        "Assigned Shards": client_data["shards"].tolist(),
        "Total Samples": len(client_data["y"]),
        **{f"Digit {digit}": class_counts[digit] for digit in range(10)}
    })

non_iid_partition_summary = pd.DataFrame(non_iid_partition_summary)

display(non_iid_partition_summary)

total_assigned_samples = sum(
    len(client_data["y"])
    for client_data in non_iid_clients.values()
)

unique_assigned_indices = np.unique(
    np.concatenate([
        client_data["indices"]
        for client_data in non_iid_clients.values()
    ])
)

print("\nVALIDATION RESULTS")
print("-" * 100)
print(f"Number of clients          : {len(non_iid_clients)}")
print(f"Number of shards           : {NUM_SHARDS}")
print(f"Shards per client          : {SHARDS_PER_CLIENT}")
print(f"Samples per client         : {[len(data['y']) for data in non_iid_clients.values()]}")
print(f"Total assigned samples     : {total_assigned_samples}")
print(f"Unique assigned samples    : {len(unique_assigned_indices)}")
print(f"Original training samples  : {len(x_train_processed)}")

partition_valid = (
    len(non_iid_clients) == NUM_CLIENTS
    and total_assigned_samples == len(x_train_processed)
    and len(unique_assigned_indices) == len(x_train_processed)
)

print(
    f"\nNon-IID partition status   : "
    f"{'Valid' if partition_valid else 'Invalid'}"
)

14. Non-IID Client Distribution and Heterogeneity Analysis¶

The class distribution of each Non-IID client is visualised and quantified. Unlike the IID setting, each client contains samples concentrated in only a limited subset of digit classes.

This analysis confirms the degree of statistical heterogeneity introduced by the shard-based partitioning and establishes the basis for comparing FedAvg performance under IID and Non-IID conditions.

15. Consolidated EDA Findings and Modelling Implications¶

The exploratory analysis confirmed that MNIST contains 60,000 training images and 10,000 testing images, with valid 28 × 28 grayscale inputs and ten digit classes. All dataset-integrity checks passed, with no missing values, infinite values, blank images, invalid labels, or out-of-range pixels.

The dataset is reasonably balanced, with class proportions close to 10% in both training and testing sets. Training and testing data also show similar pixel-intensity, foreground-density, and class-wise image characteristics, indicating no meaningful distribution mismatch between the two splits.

Approximately 81% of all pixels represent the black background, while about 19% contain handwritten foreground information. Class-average images preserve recognizable digit structures, confirming consistent centering while also showing natural handwriting variation.

The IID partition distributed all 60,000 samples equally across five clients, with similar class proportions for every client. In contrast, the Non-IID shard-based partition produced strong client heterogeneity: each client contains only three or four classes and approximately half of its data belongs to one dominant class.

Based on these findings, a CNN is selected because it can learn spatial stroke patterns effectively. Pixel values are normalized to the range 0–1, and identical preprocessing is applied to every client to ensure that local model updates remain compatible during FedAvg aggregation.

🔝 Back to Table of Contents

16. Convolutional Neural Network Model Definition¶

A compact convolutional neural network is defined for MNIST digit classification. The model contains convolution and pooling layers for spatial feature extraction, followed by dense layers for final classification.

The architecture is intentionally lightweight so that multiple client models can be trained repeatedly during federated communication rounds without excessive computational or memory requirements.

In [15]:
def create_cnn_model():
    """
    Create and compile a lightweight CNN for MNIST classification.
    A fresh model instance will be used for global and local client training.
    """
    model = tf.keras.Sequential([
        tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1)),

        tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
            filters=32,
            kernel_size=(3, 3),
            activation="relu"
        ),
        tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)),

        tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
            filters=64,
            kernel_size=(3, 3),
            activation="relu"
        ),
        tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)),

        tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),

        tf.keras.layers.Dense(
            units=64,
            activation="relu"
        ),

        tf.keras.layers.Dense(
            units=10,
            activation="softmax"
        )
    ])

    model.compile(
        optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(),
        loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
        metrics=["accuracy"]
    )

    return model

17. Local Client Training Function¶

A reusable local-training function is defined to simulate model training at an individual federated client.

At the beginning of each communication round, the client receives the latest global model weights. A fresh local model is then trained using only that client's private data. The function returns the updated model weights and the local training metrics required for subsequent FedAvg aggregation and performance reporting.

In [16]:
def train_local_client(
    global_weights,
    client_data,
    local_epochs=2,
    batch_size=32,
    verbose=0
):
    """
    Train a fresh local CNN using one client's private dataset.

    Parameters
    ----------
    global_weights : list
        Current weights received from the global model.
    client_data : dict
        Dictionary containing the client's input images and labels.
    local_epochs : int
        Number of local training epochs.
    batch_size : int
        Number of samples processed per training batch.
    verbose : int
        Keras training-output level.

    Returns
    -------
    updated_weights : list
        Locally trained model weights.
    metrics : dict
        Final local loss, accuracy, and sample count.
    """
    local_model = create_cnn_model()
    local_model.set_weights(global_weights)

    history = local_model.fit(
        client_data["x"],
        client_data["y"],
        epochs=local_epochs,
        batch_size=batch_size,
        shuffle=True,
        verbose=verbose
    )

    metrics = {
        "local_loss": float(history.history["loss"][-1]),
        "local_accuracy": float(history.history["accuracy"][-1]),
        "sample_count": len(client_data["y"])
    }

    updated_weights = local_model.get_weights()

    del local_model
    tf.keras.backend.clear_session()

    return updated_weights, metrics

18. Manual Federated Averaging Function¶

The Federated Averaging algorithm is implemented manually by combining corresponding model tensors from all participating clients. Client contributions are weighted by local sample count:

[ w_{t+1}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{n_k}{N}w_{t+1}^{(k)}, \qquad N=\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_k ]

where (K) is the number of clients, (n_k) is the number of samples held by client (k), and (w_{t+1}^{(k)}) is the locally trained parameter set returned by that client.

The implementation below validates its inputs and performs the aggregation layer by layer using NumPy. No built-in federated-learning framework is used.

In [17]:
def federated_average(client_weights, client_sample_counts):
    """
    Perform weighted Federated Averaging across client model weights.

    Parameters
    ----------
    client_weights : list
        List containing the model-weight lists returned by all clients.
    client_sample_counts : list
        Number of training samples used by each client.

    Returns
    -------
    averaged_weights : list
        Weighted-average model parameters for the updated global model.
    """
    if len(client_weights) == 0:
        raise ValueError("client_weights cannot be empty.")

    if len(client_weights) != len(client_sample_counts):
        raise ValueError(
            "The number of client-weight sets must match "
            "the number of client sample counts."
        )

    if any(sample_count <= 0 for sample_count in client_sample_counts):
        raise ValueError("All client sample counts must be positive.")

    total_samples = np.sum(client_sample_counts)

    averaged_weights = [
        np.zeros_like(layer_weights, dtype=np.float32)
        for layer_weights in client_weights[0]
    ]

    for weights, sample_count in zip(
        client_weights,
        client_sample_counts
    ):
        client_weight = sample_count / total_samples

        for layer_index, layer_weights in enumerate(weights):
            averaged_weights[layer_index] += (
                client_weight * layer_weights
            )

    return averaged_weights

19. Global Model Evaluation Function¶

A reusable evaluation function is defined to measure the global model on the complete MNIST test dataset after each communication round.

The function returns global loss and global accuracy, which are the two metrics explicitly required for round-wise federated-learning performance tracking.

In [18]:
def evaluate_global_model(model, x_test_data, y_test_data):
    """
    Evaluate the current global model on the common test dataset.

    Parameters
    ----------
    model : tf.keras.Model
        Current global CNN model.
    x_test_data : np.ndarray
        Preprocessed test images.
    y_test_data : np.ndarray
        Test labels.

    Returns
    -------
    metrics : dict
        Global loss and global accuracy.
    """
    global_loss, global_accuracy = model.evaluate(
        x_test_data,
        y_test_data,
        verbose=0
    )

    return {
        "global_loss": float(global_loss),
        "global_accuracy": float(global_accuracy)
    }

20. Implementation Assumptions¶

The following assumptions are used throughout the federated-learning implementation:

  • Five federated clients are simulated within a single Kubeflow notebook environment.
  • All five clients participate in every communication round.
  • Client communication is simulated; network latency, communication failures, and client dropouts are not modelled.
  • The MNIST training data remain logically local to each client during local training.
  • Only updated model weights and training metrics are returned from clients for aggregation.
  • The complete MNIST test dataset is retained centrally and used only to evaluate the global model.
  • All clients use the same CNN architecture, optimizer, batch size, preprocessing procedure, and initial global weights.
  • Federated Averaging is implemented manually using sample-count-weighted layer-wise aggregation.
  • The IID dataset is created through reproducible random partitioning.
  • The Non-IID dataset is created using a label-shard partitioning strategy.
  • Model training is performed sequentially for simulated clients within each communication round.

🔝 Back to Table of Contents

21. Federated Training Workflow Design¶

The federated workflow follows a synchronous, full-participation protocol. In every communication round, the server distributes the current global weights to all five clients. Each client initializes a fresh local model with those weights, trains only on its private partition, and returns its updated weights and sample count. The server then performs manual sample-weighted FedAvg and evaluates the updated global model on the common test set.

Federated Training Algorithm¶

Initialize global model w₀

For communication round t = 1, ..., 10:
    For each client k = 1, ..., 5:
        Copy global weights wₜ to a fresh local model
        Train locally for E epochs with batch size 32
        Return local weights wₜ₊₁ᵏ and sample count nₖ

    Compute N = Σₖ nₖ
    Aggregate manually:
        wₜ₊₁ = Σₖ (nₖ / N) · wₜ₊₁ᵏ

    Evaluate wₜ₊₁ on the central MNIST test set
    Record global loss, global accuracy, and client metrics

No federated-learning orchestration or aggregation library is used.

🔝 Back to Table of Contents

22. Reference Model Initialisation¶

A reference CNN is initialised once, and its weights are stored for use across all federated-learning experiments. Starting every experiment from the same model parameters ensures that comparisons between IID and Non-IID distributions and different local-epoch settings are fair and reproducible.

23. Reproducible Experiment Initialisation¶

The federated-training workflow is updated to accept a predefined set of initial model weights. This ensures that every experimental configuration begins from the same model state.

Using identical starting weights makes the comparisons between IID and Non-IID data distributions and between different local-epoch settings methodologically fair.

In [21]:
def run_federated_training(
    client_datasets,
    communication_rounds=10,
    local_epochs=2,
    batch_size=32,
    experiment_name="Federated Experiment",
    initial_weights=None,
    verbose_local_training=0
):
    """
    Run manual Federated Averaging across simulated clients.

    Parameters
    ----------
    client_datasets : dict
        Client datasets containing local images and labels.
    communication_rounds : int
        Number of federated communication rounds.
    local_epochs : int
        Number of local training epochs per client per round.
    batch_size : int
        Local training batch size.
    experiment_name : str
        Descriptive name used in printed output.
    initial_weights : list or None
        Optional reference model weights used to initialise the global model.
    verbose_local_training : int
        Keras verbosity level for local model training.

    Returns
    -------
    trained_global_model : tf.keras.Model
        Final global model after all communication rounds.
    round_history : pd.DataFrame
        Global loss and accuracy after every communication round.
    client_history : pd.DataFrame
        Client-level local loss and accuracy for every round.
    """
    if communication_rounds <= 0:
        raise ValueError("communication_rounds must be positive.")

    if local_epochs <= 0:
        raise ValueError("local_epochs must be positive.")

    if batch_size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("batch_size must be positive.")

    if not client_datasets:
        raise ValueError("client_datasets cannot be empty.")

    trained_global_model = create_cnn_model()

    if initial_weights is not None:
        trained_global_model.set_weights(
            [weight.copy() for weight in initial_weights]
        )

    round_records = []
    client_records = []

    print("=" * 100)
    print(experiment_name.upper())
    print("=" * 100)

    print(f"Communication rounds : {communication_rounds}")
    print(f"Local epochs         : {local_epochs}")
    print(f"Batch size           : {batch_size}")
    print(f"Clients              : {len(client_datasets)}")
    print(
        f"Reference weights    : "
        f"{'Applied' if initial_weights is not None else 'Not provided'}"
    )

    for round_number in range(1, communication_rounds + 1):
        current_global_weights = trained_global_model.get_weights()

        collected_client_weights = []
        client_sample_counts = []

        print(
            f"\nCommunication Round "
            f"{round_number}/{communication_rounds}"
        )
        print("-" * 100)

        for client_name, client_data in client_datasets.items():
            updated_weights, local_metrics = train_local_client(
                global_weights=current_global_weights,
                client_data=client_data,
                local_epochs=local_epochs,
                batch_size=batch_size,
                verbose=verbose_local_training
            )

            collected_client_weights.append(updated_weights)
            client_sample_counts.append(
                local_metrics["sample_count"]
            )

            client_records.append({
                "Experiment": experiment_name,
                "Round": round_number,
                "Client": client_name,
                "Local Epochs": local_epochs,
                "Sample Count": local_metrics["sample_count"],
                "Local Loss": local_metrics["local_loss"],
                "Local Accuracy": local_metrics["local_accuracy"]
            })

            print(
                f"{client_name:<10} | "
                f"Samples: {local_metrics['sample_count']:5d} | "
                f"Local Loss: {local_metrics['local_loss']:.4f} | "
                f"Local Accuracy: "
                f"{local_metrics['local_accuracy'] * 100:.2f}%"
            )

        averaged_weights = federated_average(
            collected_client_weights,
            client_sample_counts
        )

        trained_global_model.set_weights(averaged_weights)

        global_metrics = evaluate_global_model(
            trained_global_model,
            x_test_processed,
            y_test
        )

        round_records.append({
            "Experiment": experiment_name,
            "Round": round_number,
            "Local Epochs": local_epochs,
            "Global Loss": global_metrics["global_loss"],
            "Global Accuracy": global_metrics["global_accuracy"]
        })

        print(
            f"\nGlobal Loss     : "
            f"{global_metrics['global_loss']:.4f}"
        )

        print(
            f"Global Accuracy : "
            f"{global_metrics['global_accuracy'] * 100:.2f}%"
        )

    round_history = pd.DataFrame(round_records)
    client_history = pd.DataFrame(client_records)

    print("\n" + "=" * 100)
    print("FEDERATED TRAINING COMPLETED")
    print("=" * 100)

    print(f"Experiment name       : {experiment_name}")
    print(f"Communication rounds  : {communication_rounds}")
    print(f"Local epochs          : {local_epochs}")
    print(f"Batch size            : {batch_size}")
    print(f"Participating clients : {len(client_datasets)}")

    return trained_global_model, round_history, client_history

24. Main FedAvg Experiment on IID Clients¶

The primary federated-learning experiment is conducted using the IID client datasets. All five clients participate in every communication round, and each client trains locally for two epochs with a batch size of 32.

The global model is initialized using the shared reference weights. After every round, the client models are aggregated manually using sample-count-weighted FedAvg, and the updated global model is evaluated on the complete MNIST test dataset.

Observations¶

  • In Round 1, local training accuracy ranges from 96.45% to 97.09%, while the aggregated global model reaches 97.59% on the common test set.
  • Because IID clients learn from similar label distributions, their updates are directionally compatible and weighted averaging produces a strong global model.
  • Subsequent round-wise convergence is examined in Section 25.

🔝 Back to Table of Contents

25. IID Global Performance Across Communication Rounds¶

The round-wise global accuracy and loss are visualised to examine how the federated model converges under the IID client distribution.

The curves show the effect of repeated local training and FedAvg aggregation across ten communication rounds.

In [23]:
# Display round-wise IID performance
iid_round_display = iid_round_history_epoch_2.copy()

iid_round_display["Global Accuracy (%)"] = (
    iid_round_display["Global Accuracy"] * 100
)

iid_round_display = iid_round_display[
    [
        "Round",
        "Local Epochs",
        "Global Loss",
        "Global Accuracy (%)"
    ]
]

        "Global Loss": "{:.4f}",

)

26. Experiment 1A: FedAvg with One Local Epoch¶

The first local-epoch experiment trains each IID client for one epoch during every communication round.

This configuration performs less local computation before aggregation and allows the global model to receive more frequent updates relative to the amount of client-side training. Its convergence will later be compared with local epoch settings of 2 and 5.

In [24]:
iid_model_epoch_1, iid_round_history_epoch_1, iid_client_history_epoch_1 = (
    run_federated_training(
        client_datasets=iid_clients,
        communication_rounds=10,
        local_epochs=1,
        batch_size=32,
        experiment_name="IID FedAvg - Local Epoch 1",
        initial_weights=REFERENCE_INITIAL_WEIGHTS,
        verbose_local_training=0
    )
)

27. Experiment 1B: FedAvg with Five Local Epochs¶

The second local-epoch experiment trains each IID client for five epochs during every communication round.

This configuration performs more local computation before aggregation. It may improve convergence per communication round, but it also increases client-side computation and can potentially lead to stronger local model drift.

In [25]:
iid_model_epoch_5, iid_round_history_epoch_5, iid_client_history_epoch_5 = (
    run_federated_training(
        client_datasets=iid_clients,
        communication_rounds=10,
        local_epochs=5,
        batch_size=32,
        experiment_name="IID FedAvg - Local Epoch 5",
        initial_weights=REFERENCE_INITIAL_WEIGHTS,
        verbose_local_training=0
    )
)

28. Experiment 1: Comparison of Local Epoch Settings¶

The performance of FedAvg is compared for local epoch values of 1, 2, and 5 under the same IID client distribution.

All experiments use the same CNN architecture, initial weights, batch size, communication rounds, and test dataset. This controlled comparison isolates the impact of increasing the amount of local training performed before each aggregation step.

In [26]:
# Combine round-wise histories for local epoch comparison
epoch_comparison_history = pd.concat(
    [
        iid_round_history_epoch_1,
        iid_round_history_epoch_2,
        iid_round_history_epoch_5
    ],
    ignore_index=True
)

# Build final summary table
epoch_summary_records = []

for epoch_value, history in [
    (1, iid_round_history_epoch_1),
    (2, iid_round_history_epoch_2),
    (5, iid_round_history_epoch_5)
]:
    best_accuracy_row = history.loc[
        history["Global Accuracy"].idxmax()
    ]

    lowest_loss_row = history.loc[
        history["Global Loss"].idxmin()
    ]

    epoch_summary_records.append({
        "Local Epochs": epoch_value,
        "Round 1 Accuracy (%)": (
            history.iloc[0]["Global Accuracy"] * 100
        ),
        "Final Accuracy (%)": (
            history.iloc[-1]["Global Accuracy"] * 100
        ),
        "Best Accuracy (%)": (
            best_accuracy_row["Global Accuracy"] * 100
        ),
        "Best Accuracy Round": int(
            best_accuracy_row["Round"]
        ),
        "Final Loss": history.iloc[-1]["Global Loss"],
        "Lowest Loss": lowest_loss_row["Global Loss"],
        "Lowest Loss Round": int(
            lowest_loss_row["Round"]
        )
    })

epoch_comparison_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    epoch_summary_records
)

print("=" * 110)
print("LOCAL EPOCH COMPARISON SUMMARY")
print("=" * 110)

display(
    epoch_comparison_summary.style.format({
        "Round 1 Accuracy (%)": "{:.2f}%",
        "Final Accuracy (%)": "{:.2f}%",
        "Best Accuracy (%)": "{:.2f}%",
        "Final Loss": "{:.4f}",
        "Lowest Loss": "{:.4f}"
    })
)

# Accuracy comparison
plt.figure(figsize=(11, 6))

for epoch_value, history in [
    (1, iid_round_history_epoch_1),
    (2, iid_round_history_epoch_2),
    (5, iid_round_history_epoch_5)
]:
    plt.plot(
        history["Round"],
        history["Global Accuracy"] * 100,
        marker="o",
        label=f"Local Epochs = {epoch_value}"
    )

plt.title("Global Accuracy Comparison for Different Local Epochs")
plt.xlabel("Communication Round")
plt.ylabel("Global Accuracy (%)")
plt.xticks(range(1, 11))
plt.legend()

30.1 Proxy Analysis of Client Drift: Dispersion of Local Training Accuracy¶

Client drift is fundamentally a divergence in local model updates under heterogeneous data. Directly measuring weight-vector divergence would require storing every client's full update tensor for every round. As a lightweight diagnostic, this notebook compares the round-wise standard deviation of local training accuracy across the five clients.

A higher dispersion indicates that clients are progressing differently on their local objectives. This is used only as a proxy for heterogeneous client behavior, not as a direct measurement of parameter-space drift.

In [29]:
# Quantify client drift as the round-wise standard deviation of local
# client accuracy. A HIGHER standard deviation means the five clients'
# locally trained models disagree more with each other before aggregation.

iid_dispersion = (
    iid_client_history_epoch_2
    .groupby("Round")["Local Accuracy"]
    .std()
    .rename("IID Client Accuracy Std Dev (%)") * 100
)

non_iid_dispersion = (
    non_iid_client_history_epoch_2
    .groupby("Round")["Local Accuracy"]
    .std()
    .rename("Non-IID Client Accuracy Std Dev (%)") * 100
)

dispersion_comparison = pd.concat(
    [iid_dispersion, non_iid_dispersion], axis=1
)

print("=" * 110)
print("CLIENT DRIFT: DISPERSION OF LOCAL ACCURACY ACROSS CLIENTS PER ROUND")
print("=" * 110)

display(
    dispersion_comparison.style.format("{:.3f}")
)

plt.figure(figsize=(11, 6))

plt.plot(
    dispersion_comparison.index,
    dispersion_comparison["IID Client Accuracy Std Dev (%)"],
    marker="o",
    label="IID"
)

plt.plot(
    dispersion_comparison.index,
    dispersion_comparison["Non-IID Client Accuracy Std Dev (%)"],
    marker="o",
    label="Non-IID"
)

plt.title(
    "Client Drift: Standard Deviation of Local Client Accuracy "
    "per Communication Round"
)
plt.xlabel("Communication Round")
plt.ylabel("Standard Deviation of Local Accuracy (percentage points)")
plt.xticks(range(1, 11))
plt.legend()
plt.grid(linestyle="--", alpha=0.4)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

mean_iid_dispersion = dispersion_comparison["IID Client Accuracy Std Dev (%)"].mean()
mean_non_iid_dispersion = dispersion_comparison["Non-IID Client Accuracy Std Dev (%)"].mean()

print("\nSUMMARY")
print("-" * 110)
print(f"Mean IID client-accuracy std dev     : {mean_iid_dispersion:.3f} pp")
print(f"Mean Non-IID client-accuracy std dev : {mean_non_iid_dispersion:.3f} pp")
print(
    f"Non-IID clients disagree with each other, on average, "
    f"{mean_non_iid_dispersion / mean_iid_dispersion:.2f}x more than IID clients."
    if mean_iid_dispersion > 0 else ""
)

32. Consolidated Experimental Findings¶

The IID configuration converged rapidly. With two local epochs, global accuracy increased from 97.59% in Round 1 to 99.28% after ten rounds, with the lowest loss of 0.0254 also occurring in Round 10.

The local-epoch comparison produced final accuracies of 99.10%, 99.28%, and 99.26% for 1, 2, and 5 local epochs respectively. Five epochs achieved the highest intermediate accuracy (99.30% at Round 9), but two epochs delivered the strongest final result in this rerun with lower computational cost than five epochs.

The Non-IID model improved from 41.06% to 78.76%, but remained 20.52 percentage points below the IID model. Local client training accuracies remained near 100%, demonstrating that client-level fit can coexist with weak global generalization when label distributions are highly skewed.

Class-wise results confirm uneven Non-IID performance. Digit 5 is the most affected class, with its F1-score falling from 0.990 under IID training to 0.317 under Non-IID training.

🔝 Back to Table of Contents

33. Critical Analysis¶

Why does FedAvg perform differently on IID and Non-IID data?¶

IID clients contain similar class proportions, so their local objectives and updates are broadly aligned. This produced rapid and stable convergence to 99.28% global accuracy.

Non-IID clients are dominated by different labels, causing local specialization and conflicting updates. Although local training accuracy remained near 100%, the global model reached only 78.76%, demonstrating weaker generalization.

What is the impact of increasing local epochs?¶

More local epochs improve the amount of learning completed before each communication event. In this experiment, five epochs improved early-round accuracy but finished at 99.26%, slightly below the two-epoch result of 99.28%, while requiring 2.5 times as much local training per round.

Therefore, additional local epochs can reduce communication needs but may provide diminishing returns and, under Non-IID data, can intensify client specialization.

Improvement over Standard FedAvg¶

FedProx adds a proximal term to each client's local objective, penalizing large deviation from the current global weights. This can reduce local drift and improve stability under heterogeneous client distributions. This assignment identifies FedProx as the appropriate extension for improving stability under heterogeneous client distributions; its implementation remains outside the defined assignment scope.

🔝 Back to Table of Contents

34. Limitations and Practical Considerations¶

The implementation successfully demonstrates the FedAvg workflow, but it represents a controlled simulation rather than a production federated-learning deployment.

  • All five clients are simulated sequentially within one Kubeflow environment rather than running on physically separate systems.
  • All clients participate in every communication round; client dropout and partial participation are not considered.
  • Communication latency, network failures, bandwidth consumption, and model-transfer cost are not measured.
  • All clients have equal dataset sizes and identical computing capacity.
  • The Non-IID distribution is intentionally strong and is created using label-based shards.
  • Only the standard FedAvg algorithm is implemented; methods such as FedProx are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.
  • Privacy mechanisms such as secure aggregation, encryption, and differential privacy are outside the scope of this assignment.
  • The experiment uses MNIST and a lightweight CNN, so the results may not directly represent larger real-world medical-image datasets.

🔝 Back to Table of Contents

35. Conclusion¶

This assignment implemented Federated Averaging manually for MNIST image classification using five simulated clients. Both IID and label-shard Non-IID partitions were evaluated without using TensorFlow Federated, Flower, FedML, PySyft, or any other federated-learning framework.

Under IID data, the two-local-epoch configuration reached 99.28% global accuracy and 0.0254 loss after ten communication rounds. Increasing local epochs to five improved early-round learning but did not improve the final result, illustrating diminishing returns from additional client-side computation.

Under Non-IID data, final global accuracy was 78.76%, producing a 20.52 percentage-point gap relative to the equivalent IID run. The class-wise analysis showed substantial bias, particularly for digit 5.

The results demonstrate that standard FedAvg performs strongly when client distributions are similar but is sensitive to severe statistical heterogeneity. FedProx or related drift-control methods are appropriate directions for future work.
